summary: Describes LDP protocol extensions needed to support multi-topology routing in an MPLS environment, extending MT support from IGPs to label distribution.

eli5.summary: One network can have several maps for different kinds of traffic. This lets label distribution use those separate maps.

questions: what is an mt-id in mpls
how does ldp advertise multi-topology capability
what does invalid topology id mean in ldp
subtitle: How MPLS Label Distribution Protocol learns to keep separate label bindings for separate network topologies.

tldr.problem: IP networks can run several routing topologies using MT-aware IGPs, but LDP had no way to bind labels within a particular topology.
tldr.mechanism: Two new address families, MT IP and MT IPv6, add a 16-bit MT-ID to prefix FEC elements, and a new Multi-Topology capability lets peers announce support.
tldr.outcome: LDP can set up label switched paths per topology within a single session. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 9658.

today: RFC 7307 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9658. The unit metadata does not list it as obsoleted.

sections.title: Why MPLS Needs Multi-Topology
sections.content:
Multi-Topology (MT) routing is supported in IP networks with MT-aware IGPs. The RFC argues it would help Communications Service Providers to have an MPLS multi-topology environment, and lists uses: different Quality of Service profiles per traffic class, isolating multicast and IPv6 islands, routing specific address space for security or operational isolation, assigning low-latency links to delay-sensitive traffic, and separating management traffic from customer traffic.

The document describes the LDP procedures and protocol extensions needed to support this, and defines two new FEC types for LSP ping.
sections.eli5: A network can have different roads for different jobs, like fast lanes for urgent mail. This RFC teaches the label system about those separate roads.

sections.title: Topology-Scoped FEC and the MT-ID
sections.content:
LDP assigns a label to a FEC (Forwarding Equivalence Class), a list of one or more FEC elements, and advertises it to peers so a path is set up along the routing path. For multi-topology, the prefix-related FEC element is extended so that the MT-ID becomes one of its attributes. All FEC-label binding is then done in the context of a given topology.

The MT-ID is a 16-bit value. The default topology uses MT-ID 0, and that value MUST be ignored on receipt so it does not conflict with existing non-MT procedures.
sections.eli5: Each label now also carries a tag saying which map it belongs to, and the default map is tag zero.

sections.title: MT Address Families and FEC Elements
sections.content:
Two new address families, MT IP and MT IPv6, specify IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes within a topology scope. Their data is the address followed by a 16-bit Reserved field and a 16-bit MT-ID. They can be used in any LDP message and procedure that allows FEC elements with the IP or IPv6 address family.

The MT Prefix FEC element carries Prefix (2), the address family, PreLen, the prefix, then Reserved and MT-ID. The MT Typed Wildcard FEC element (type 5) carries a FEC type, a length of 6, the address family and an MT-ID. The only FEC type allowed in it here is the Prefix FEC element.
sections.eli5: The address gets two extra pieces at the end, a spare slot and the map tag, so the label knows which map the address belongs to.

sections.title: Advertising the MT Capability
sections.content:
A new LDP capability named Multi-Topology is defined following the LDP capability guidelines of RFC 5561. It is carried in a Multi-Topology Capability TLV with the U-bit set to 1, the F-bit set to 0, and one or more Typed Wildcard FEC elements as capability data. Their MT-ID MUST be set to the Wildcard Topology. An LDP speaker MUST NOT send messages containing MT FEC elements unless the peer has said it can handle them.

The capability can be advertised in the LDP Initialization message, or later in a Capability message if Dynamic Capability Announcement has been negotiated. The S-bit MUST be 1 in an Initialization message. If an LSR does not support Dynamic Capability Announcement, it MUST reset the session whenever its local MT capability changes.
sections.eli5: Before using the new tags, a router tells its neighbor it understands them. Nobody sends tags to a neighbor that has not said it is ready.

sections.title: Label Spaces, Wildcards and LSP Ping
sections.content:
Multiple topologies do not need different label spaces; an LSR can use the same label space for all MT FECs as for the default topology, and signaling for different topologies can and should be done within a single LDP session. Forwarding is outside the scope, but the RFC notes that the data plane cannot tie a received packet to one topology, so topology-specific label spaces cannot be used.

Typed Wildcard operations can be scoped to one topology, for example withdrawing all labels for a de-configured topology, or use the Wildcard Topology MT-ID to cover all topologies. The completion signaling of RFC 5919 applies per topology.

For LSP ping (RFC 4379), two new Target FEC Stack sub-types are defined: 31 for MT LDP IPv4 and 32 for MT LDP IPv6. If the return path is not specified, the reply goes through the default topology.
sections.eli5: All the maps share one pile of labels and one conversation. A router can also ask to forget the labels for one map or for all maps at once.

sections.title: Errors and Backwards Compatibility
sections.content:
The extensions use the existing LDP error handling of RFC 5036. An LSR that receives an LDP message with a FEC element naming an MT-ID that is not locally known or not supported should respond with an Invalid Topology ID status code in a Notification message, and MUST discard the entire message first. An LSR that receives an unassigned MT-ID MUST abort processing of that FEC element.

The solution is backwards compatible with the LDP enhancements of RFC 5036, and a legacy node that does not support MT should not receive any MT-related messages.
sections.eli5: If a router gets a tag for a map it has never heard of, it throws the message away and politely says so.

sections.title: IANA Assignments and the MT-ID Registry
sections.content:
IANA assigned the Multi-Topology Capability TLV (0x050C), the status code Invalid Topology ID (0x00000031), and address family numbers 29 (MT IP) and 30 (MT IPv6). A new registry, MPLS Multi-Topology Identifiers, records MT-ID values, and the sub-types 31 and 32 were registered for LSP ping.

The RFC says a separate document will detail the policy for allocating new MT-ID values.
sections.eli5: An official list records what each map number means, so everyone uses the same numbers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that using MT over existing MPLS solutions does not offer any specific security benefit. General LDP communication threats, namely spoofing, privacy and denial of service, are described in RFC 5036, and further discussion is pointed to RFC 5920.
sections.eli5: Adding extra maps does not make the system any safer or any less safe than before.

fields.name: MT-ID
fields.desc: The 16-bit topology ID for the address.
